lifecycle_control.reason: A logical node becomes unavailable via Raft.Shutdown() (closes shutdownCh, sets state Shutdown, and the returned future blocks until all background goroutines exit via routinesGroup.Wait) and becomes available again by constructing a new Raft with NewRaft over the same caller-owned LogStore/StableStore/SnapshotStore/FSM. This is an honest stop/reconstruction cycle: a new instance is constructed on restart; Shutdown is not a crash and no crash-recovery semantics are invented. A second, softer availability mechanism exists: InmemTransport Connect/Disconnect/DisconnectAll (and the cluster harness Partition/Disconnect/FullyConnect) isolate or rejoin a running node without stopping it.
limitations: Honest semantics: restart constructs a new Raft instance; Shutdown is not a pause and no crash/persistence/recovery behavior beyond the caller-provided stores is claimed.
Out-of-boundary: process supervision, crash injection, and durable store implementations are not part of the module.

lifecycle_control.test_support_reason: Shutdown plus NewRaft with the same caller-owned stores is a directly usable stop/restart composition, and Connect/Disconnect provides pause/resume-like availability control; the in-package harness (cluster.Close, Partition, FullyConnect) demonstrates both.
execution_paths: shutdown_restart: Raft.Shutdown() (unavailable: state=Shutdown, all goroutines exited) then NewRaft(conf, fsm, logs, stable, snaps, trans) with the same caller-owned stores (available again; new instance with restored persisted state).

availability_partition: InmemTransport Disconnect/DisconnectAll (node isolated, still running) and Connect (node rejoins); cluster harness Partition/Disconnect/FullyConnect compose the same operations.

message_capture.gap: No dedicated controlled cache with explicit Enumerate/Take/Drop/Clear; capture channel is shared with the node's main loop (race on delivery); external consumers cannot requeue captured requests into the receive-only channel; no peek operation.
message_capture.reason: The per-node InmemTransport consumer channel (Consumer() -> <-chan RPC, consumed by the Raft main loop as rpcCh) is a working interception point for every protocol message family: a test can receive (take) an RPC holding Command, Reader, and RespChan, hold it (delaying delivery to the node), drain (enumerate/clear), or drop it, and the package's own tests prove this pattern. However, per the test contract this is an observable channel, i.e. a primitive: it is shared with the node's main loop (the test races the protocol consumer), there is no explicit take/drop/clear cache API, no peek, and external (non-in-package) consumers cannot requeue a captured request into the receive-only channel. A low-intrusion wrapper (exported intercepting transport or a testing.go capture cache) completes the capability.
limitations: Analysis covers the in-boundary InmemTransport path; NetworkTransport/TCP behavior is out of boundary and not evaluated.

InmemTransport.SetHeartbeatHandler is a no-op (inmem_transport.go:74), so heartbeats flow through the consumer channel and are capturable there; other transports may fast-path heartbeats outside this channel.
message_capture.suggested_direction: Complete a thin test-visible cache over the existing consumer channel; no protocol behavior change needed.
usage_examples:

if req.Term != wantTerm { t.Fatalf("unexpected message: %+v", req) }
message_capture.test_support_reason: The consumer channel is a primitive under the contract: it is an observable channel shared with the protocol consumer, so guaranteed retention-before-delivery, explicit Take/Drop/Clear operations, and external requeue of captured requests are not provided by the target API; only the raw intercept mechanics exist (proven by transport_test.go and inmem_transport_test.go).
suggested_changes: Add an exported intercepting/capture transport (or a testing.go helper) that drains InmemTransport.Consumer() into a test-owned cache of RPC instances and exposes Enumerate, Take (removing one RPC and returning it with RespChan), Drop, and Clear, plus a requeue operation that puts the RPC back on the channel so delivery to the node resumes only on a test action.
Optionally extend MakeClusterOpts/cluster so each node's transport is pre-wired through the capture cache, giving tests a stable handle per node without racing the main loop.
execution_paths: inbound_rpc: per-node InmemTransport consumerCh. Protocol output: RPC requests from peers (RequestVote, RequestPreVote, AppendEntries incl. heartbeats, InstallSnapshot, TimeoutNow) enqueued via makeRPC; delivery to the node automatically continues when the main loop reads rpcCh, and is paused whenever the test holds a taken RPC (the sender blocks on RespChan). Cache owner: the InmemTransport instance (channel buffer, cap 16). Enumerate: drain with select/default; Take: receive one RPC; Drop: receive and ignore or Respond(err); Clear: drain loop. Normal input boundary: trans.Consumer() -> rpcCh -> processRPC. Consumer scope: any test holding the *InmemTransport (public Consumer()); in-package tests additionally reach the private field. Injection pairing: separated Take plus Respond/requeue; no combined single-call facade.

append_pipeline: pipelined AppendEntries from a leader replication loop. Requests traverse the same peer consumerCh capture point (inmemPipeline.AppendEntries enqueues an RPC there), so capture is identical to inbound_rpc; responses are decoded by inmemPipeline.decodeResponses into the pipeline's doneCh (pipeline.Consumer() -> <-chan AppendFuture). A test intercepting at the peer's consumerCh controls both the request and its response via rpc.Respond.

evidence.reason: Normal response input operation: sends RPCResponse{resp, err} on RespChan, completing the original sender.

The normal protocol input boundary that consumes injected requests from rpcCh.

message_injection.gap: No combined single-call injection facade; external consumers cannot requeue a captured RPC into the receive-only consumer channel without a peer-transport reconstruction (which orphans the original sender's RespChan, though the timeout effect is explicit); cache effects are implicit.
message_injection.reason: Injection operates on the same inbound_rpc path as capture: the separated form works today - a test takes an RPC from the consumer channel and either calls rpc.Respond (the documented normal response input, preserving routing via RespChan) or re-delivers the request through the channel (in-package) or via a peer transport send (external). Successful delivery completes the sender's makeRPC with the response copied back; synchronous failure is Respond(resp, err) causing makeRPC to return the error; unconfirmed asynchronous delivery lets the sender time out after the InmemTransport timeout (default 500ms) - all cache effects are explicit. The gap is that no combined single-call facade exists and requeue of captured requests is not a public operation, so a low-intrusion wrapper over the same cache completes the capability.
limitations: Injection analysis is scoped to InmemTransport inside the boundary; TCP/network transport behavior is out of boundary.
A test that drops a captured request must account for the sender's 500ms default InmemTransport timeout (NewInmemTransport, inmem_transport.go:68-70).
message_injection.suggested_direction: Pair the capture cache with an inject/requeue operation on the same path; no protocol changes required.
usage_examples:

message_injection.test_support_reason: The separated form (take from the consumer channel plus Respond / peer-send) is directly usable and proven by package tests, but injection is not a complete public interface: there is no combined single-call operation binding a cached message to its target, requeue of captured requests is not exposed (receive-only channel externally), and cache-state effects are implicit rather than declared.
suggested_changes: Extend the same capture-cache wrapper with an inject method that requeues a taken RPC onto the node's consumer channel (preserving Command/Reader/RespChan) or responds on behalf of the node, so take-plus-input is a documented single operation on the same cache instance.
Document cache effects (success, synchronous failure, unconfirmed async timeout) on the wrapper's Take and inject operations.
execution_paths: inbound_rpc: normal input boundary is trans.Consumer() -> rpcCh -> processRPC. Separated injection: Take from the capture cache, then rpc.Respond (responses, preserving RespChan routing) or requeue/deliver the request to the same channel (in-package write; external via a peer transport's AppendEntries/RequestVote/InstallSnapshot which reconstructs the RPC and routes to the same consumerCh). Cache effects: success - taken RPC removed, sender completes; synchronous failure - Respond(err) returns error to sender; unconfirmed async - sender times out (send/command timeout, inmem_transport.go:183-198). No combined single-call facade exists.

append_pipeline: same capture point; a test Respond on the intercepted RPC feeds inmemPipeline.decodeResponses, which copies the response into the appendFuture and publishes it to doneCh; the pipeline future's completion mechanism (AppendFuture) is preserved.

randomness_control.reason: Protocol-relevant randomness is the randomized timeout staggering: randomTimeout (util.go:34) draws from the process-global math/rand (rand.Int63) to produce [minVal, 2*minVal), used for election timeouts, heartbeat timeouts, commit staggering, and snapshot intervals. Because the choice is exposed through the global rand source, a test can fix it with rand.Seed(fixed) before starting nodes, and the minimum of the range is configurable (Config.ElectionTimeout, HeartbeatTimeout, CommitTimeout, SnapshotInterval), so the same initial state and control parameters reproduce the same random choices without replacing the algorithm or changing the production default (init() crypto-seeds the global source at process start). Scope is shared/process-global, which is documented as a limitation.
limitations: Control scope is process-global/shared across all nodes; per-node or per-instance randomness control is not available without target changes (a config-injected rand source would be a low-intrusion future option).
Reproducibility depends on the rand call sequence; other packages in the process consuming math/rand can perturb it.
crypto/rand-based UUIDs for in-memory addresses (NewInmemAddr/generateUUID) are not controllable, but they do not affect protocol decisions.
usage_examples:

conf := raft.DefaultConfig()
conf.ElectionTimeout = 200 * time.Millisecond // deterministic lower bound; draw range [200ms, 400ms)
// same seed + same timeouts => same random election/heartbeat/snapshot staggering sequence
randomness_control.test_support_reason: The random choice is reachable through the standard global rand source that the target uses; a test seeds it directly (no target change) and configures the range minimum, reproducing the same choices for the same seed and call sequence.
execution_paths: global_rand_election_timeout: randomTimeout consumes the process-global math/rand; tests fix it with math/rand.Seed(seed) and set Config timeouts; scope is shared across all nodes in the process (documented), domain [minVal, 2*minVal) preserved. Other randomization (NewInmemAddr UUIDs via crypto/rand, generateUUID) is address-only and not protocol-relevant.

time_control.gap: No explicit Tick and no injectable Clock; wall-clock time is used directly across all protocol state loops and replication.
time_control.reason: The protocol observes time exclusively through dispersed wall-clock calls: randomTimeout returns time.After(minVal+extra) (util.go:39), follower/candidate/leader loops use time.After/time.Now (raft.go:163, 217, 310, 677, 728, 749), replication uses time.After backoff and time.Now (replication.go:131, 213, 230, 343, 411), snapshot and log-store metric loops use time.After (snapshot.go:75, log.go:180), and saturation/metrics use time.Now (saturation.go:47). There is no explicit Tick method and no injectable Clock type anywhere in the package (no Clock symbol exists). Per the v0.1 rule, dispersed wall-clock use without explicit Tick or injectable Clock is INVASIVE: deterministic advancement cannot be provided without restructuring time usage throughout the main loops.
limitations: Deterministic time advancement is currently achievable only by composing real-time waits with short configured timeouts (the in-package harness uses 50ms timeouts, testing.go:26-28); this does not manufacture protocol outcomes deterministically.
Out-of-boundary: fuzzy and raft-compat subdirectories (not analyzed) contain their own time handling.
time_control.suggested_direction: Add an injectable clock with the real clock as the unchanged production default; any route requires touching the main loops, hence INVASIVE for v0.1.
time_control.test_support_reason: No Tick or injectable Clock exists; all timers are created and consumed inside the main loops from wall clock, so tests cannot deterministically advance protocol-observed time without intrusive restructuring.
suggested_changes: Introduce an injectable clock abstraction (e.g., a now()/after() indirection on Config, defaulting to the real clock) and route randomTimeout and all time.After/time.Now call sites through it; tests then supply a manual clock.
Alternatively expose an explicit Tick-style hook, which requires the same restructuring of the follower/candidate/leader select loops.
execution_paths: wall_clock_timers: all protocol timing (heartbeat/election timeouts, leader lease, commit staggering, snapshot interval, replication backoff) derives from time.After/time.Now with no injectable seam; no accepted v0.1 form (explicit Tick or injectable Clock) exists.
